Okay, the last few attempts to bring the server up have been messy. I first added error handling to the WebSocket server, then changed the listen logic to use a `'listening'` event instead of the callback, hoping that would prevent the double‑banner issue. After that I tried to restart the server, but the background job from the earlier `nohup` command was still alive, so the first restart still hit a busy port and fell back to the next one (3001, then 3002). 

When I finally killed the stale process with `pkill -f "node server/index.js"` and restarted, the command returned an exit code 144, indicating the kill didn't succeed cleanly—perhaps some instance is still hanging. My subsequent check (`sleep 1; cat /tmp/glint.log; curl ...`) again showed the server binding to 3002 after reporting that 3000 and 3001 were busy. The curl to `/api/games` now failed to return valid JSON, throwing a `JSONDecodeError`. That tells me the HTTP request either got no response or got something non‑JSON (maybe an error page) because the server never fully started or is bound to a different port than I’m querying.

So the core problem is that I don’t actually know which process is holding ports 3000, 3001, or 3002 at this moment. I need to investigate the port usage on the system (e.g., `lsof -i :3000` etc.) to identify the stray Node processes or any other service. Before I dive into more code changes, I should surface this uncertainty to the user: we have port confusion and need to check who holds which ports. That will guide the next debugging step.
